lessons.title: From click to database
lessons.body:
A web application has three cooperating layers: the interface, the server, and persistent storage.

The browser sends an HTTP request. The API authenticates the user, validates input, applies business rules, and queries the database. The response updates the interface.

Lab: sketch the request flow for joining a course. Mark the point at which authorization must be checked.

lessons.title: Design a useful API
lessons.body:
Represent resources with clear routes. Use GET for reads and POST for creation. Validate input on the server even when the interface also validates it.

Use 401 for missing authentication, 403 for denied access, 404 for missing resources, and 409 for conflicts.

Lab: define endpoints and response shapes for a campus lost-and-found service.

lessons.title: Store data with intent
lessons.body:
Give each entity a stable ID. Relate enrollments to both users and courses. Unique constraints stop duplicate relationships even under simultaneous requests.

Never store plaintext passwords. Treat authorization and data validation as server responsibilities.

Lab: draw the tables or collections for your project and identify three invariants.

lessons.title: Model the boundary
lessons.body:
Inputs from HTTP are untrusted. Validate required fields, types, lengths, and allowed values before using them.

Separate request handling, business rules, and persistence. This makes each responsibility easier to explain and test.

Lab: validate an assignment submission containing a text response and an optional HTTPS repository URL.

lessons.title: Transactions and invariants
lessons.body:
A transaction groups related database changes. Either all changes commit, or none do.

Joining a team and recording membership should not leave a half-created result. Unique constraints are a second line of defense.

Lab: write a test that sends the same enrollment twice.

lessons.title: Test behavior, not screenshots
lessons.body:
API tests should exercise success and failure. Verify authentication, ownership, empty values, deadlines, and repeated requests.

Lab: test that a student cannot publish a course and that an instructor cannot grade another instructor’s assignment.

lessons.title: Choose one painful problem
lessons.body:
Talk to a potential user before designing a large feature list. Describe one problem, one audience, and one observable improvement.

Lab: write a three-sentence problem statement. Record what is assumed and what is verified.

lessons.title: Build the smallest complete journey
lessons.body:
A complete vertical slice lets someone accomplish a real task. Build sign-in, one useful workflow, persistence, and a clear result before adding extras.

Lab: divide your team by ownership and agree on API shapes before implementation.

lessons.title: Tell a credible demo story
lessons.body:
Start with the user’s problem. Show the working flow. Explain your architecture, one technical tradeoff, and what you would build next.

Credit dependencies and teammates. Keep a local fallback ready in case the network fails.

Lab: rehearse a three-minute demo with another team.

options: On the server for each protected operation
questions.explanation: Clients can be modified. The server must enforce access rules.

questions.prompt: Which status means a resource conflicts with existing state?
questions.explanation: 409 signals a conflict such as an existing enrollment.
Database constraints remain effective when requests race.

options: Related changes commit together or roll back
questions.explanation: Transactions preserve consistency across related writes.
Browser validation does not establish trust.

questions.prompt: What is the best first delivery target?
questions.explanation: A complete journey proves the system works end to end.

questions.prompt: What belongs in a credible demo?
questions.explanation: Judges should be able to verify your claims.
